rows.label: Life satisfaction lost per year in prison or jail (points, 0-10)

source.title: World Database of Happiness, Pappot & Phaff (2004): study NL 2004 (prisoners and controls, the Netherlands)
source.page: general happiness and momentary mood, recoded to 0-10
source.note: Momentary mood, asked three times a day for ten days: prisoners 5.25, controls 6.73. Small non-probability sample (N = 42, 40% non-response). Chason (1975, US, World Database of Happiness) found prisoners at 1.23 on a 1-3 life-satisfaction item against 2.22 for the general population, about half the scale; a systematic review of quality-of-life assessments of offenders (vLex, Law Journals) finds detained offenders below the general population.

rows.explainer: What a year in prison or jail costs a person in life satisfaction, against a year outside. No study found asks prisoners the 0-10 life-satisfaction question beside a comparison group, so happiness and mood stand in for it: 0.77 points of general happiness and 1.48 of momentary mood in the one 0-10 comparison found (42 Dutch prisoners and controls, 2004), about half the scale in an older US survey. US prisons are harsher than Dutch ones, but the controls weren't matched to people who would otherwise be in prison and happiness is not life satisfaction, so the range is wide: 1.2, from 0.5 to 3. Read by every model that counts years of incarceration averted or freedom won (WELLBYs: a point for a year is one).

rows.label: Years of life lost per year in prison (New York State parolees)

source.title: Patterson (2013), The dose-response of time served in prison on mortality: New York State, 1989-2003, American Journal of Public Health 103(3): 523-528
source.quote: each additional year in prison produced a 15.6% increase in the odds of death for parolees, which translated to a 2-year decline in life expectancy for each year served in prison

rows.explainer: New York parolees, 1989-2003: 2 years of life expectancy lost per year served. Observational, with longer sentences going to people at higher risk anyway, so the low end is a quarter of it (0.5); high 3. This is mortality, the years a person does not live; the life-satisfaction figure (ls_loss_per_year_incarcerated) is the wellbeing of the years they do live, so a model counting both counts different things. Read by every model that counts years of incarceration averted.

rows.label: Remaining life expectancy of a person in prison (years)

source.title: charityevals' judgment, anchored on Patterson (2013)'s example: about 10 years of life lost for a man of 30 serving 5 years
source.note: People in US prisons are mostly in their thirties and forties; the remaining life expectancy is our judgment (40 years, 33 to 47), not a figure from the paper.

rows.explainer: People in US prisons are mostly in their thirties and forties, with life expectancy below the general population's: 40 years left (33 to 47). Turns years of life lost into a share of a death.

rows.label: Years from a prison-year until the deaths it causes

source.title: Patterson (2013), The dose-response of time served in prison on mortality: New York State, 1989-2003, American Journal of Public Health 103(3): 523-528
source.note: The excess risk is 'highest upon release from prison and declined over time'; the delay is our judgment.

rows.explainer: The excess risk is 'highest upon release from prison and declined over time' (Patterson 2013), recovering over about two thirds of the time served: the rest of the sentence plus a few years after release, 3 years (1 to 8). The deaths come this long after the prison-year, so a model discounts them for the wait.

rows.label: Deaths caused per year of pretrial jail, as a share of the deaths per year in prison

source.title: charityevals' judgment, anchored on Patterson (2013), The dose-response of time served in prison on mortality: New York State, 1989-2003, American Journal of Public Health 103(3): 523-528
source.note: Patterson's figure is a dose-response across prison terms that all end in release, so it prices time inside. Khatri et al., JAMA Network Open 2025 (reported by Prison Policy Initiative, 24 June 2025): 4.6 more deaths per 100,000 county residents for each 10% higher jail incarceration rate, an ecological association, an upper cross-check. Deaths in jail come early: drug and alcohol deaths a median of a day after admission, suicides within about nine days (Adler and Chen, Health Affairs 2023, secondary reports).

rows.explainer: The site's years of life lost per year incarcerated come from a dose-response across New York prison terms, all ending in release; a bailout is itself a release, so what it removes is time inside, priced pro rata at 1. Two things lower it for weeks in a county jail: the deaths in jail cluster in the first days after admission (overdoses and withdrawal, suicides), mostly before a charitable bail is posted, and a few weeks bring less of the cumulative harm to health, work and family that drives deaths after long terms. Our judgment: half the prison rate per year (0.1 to 1.2); Khatri et al.'s county association (ecological) would allow more. Read by every model that counts days of pretrial detention avoided.

rows.label: Jail costs a US county saves per day a person isn't held (marginal, US$)

source.title: charityevals' judgment, anchored on The Bail Project, 2025 Annual Report: $107 million of taxpayer savings over 1,381,170 days of pretrial incarceration prevented
source.note: $107 million over 1,381,170 days is $77 a day, an average cost of a jail bed; the cost that varies with the count is lower.

rows.explainer: What a county saves when one fewer person is held for a day: food, medical care and the staff and space that vary with the count, below the average cost of about $77 a day that charitable bail funds quote. Our judgment: $35 (15 to 80). Read by every model that counts jail days avoided.

rows.label: Formal earnings gained a year by a defendant released before trial rather than detained, three to four years later (US$)

source.title: Dobbie, Goldin and Yang (2016), The Effects of Pre-Trial Detention on Conviction, Future Crime, and Employment: Evidence from Randomly Assigned Judges, NBER Working Paper 22511 (American Economic Review 108(2), 2018)
source.quote: Formal sector earnings are $1,024 higher over the same time period, a 17.5 percent increase from the mean
source.note: The same table's least-squares estimate with baseline earnings controls is $224; the two-stage estimate's standard error is $1,338, and household income shows no gain.

rows.explainer: Released defendants in Philadelphia and Miami are 10.2 points more likely to be in formal work three to four years on, mostly because fewer are convicted. Earnings: $1,024 a year (not significant) by judge assignment, $224 by least squares with controls, and no gain in household income, so some formal pay replaces informal work: $500 a year (0 to 2,000), in the paper's dollars of the early 2010s, left unadjusted for inflation since the range is far wider. Jobs lost during detention are in it. Read by every model that counts defendants released.

rows.label: How long released defendants' better employment holds (years)

source.title: charityevals' judgment, anchored on Dobbie, Goldin and Yang (2016), NBER Working Paper 22511
source.quote: we find that pre-trial release also increases the probability of employment in the formal labor market three to four years after the bail hearing by 10.2 percentage points

rows.explainer: Measured three to four years after the bail hearing; a conviction's mark on employment lasts longer, but the gain is imprecise. Our judgment: 4 years (2 to 10). Read with release_earnings_gain.

rows.label: Days of post-conviction jail or prison avoided per defendant released before trial rather than detained

source.title: charityevals' judgment, anchored on Heaton, Mayson and Stevenson (2017), The Downstream Consequences of Misdemeanor Pretrial Detention, Stanford Law Review 69: 711, and Dobbie, Goldin and Yang (2016), NBER Working Paper 22511
source.quote: are 43% more likely to be sentenced to jail
source.note: Heaton et al. (Harris County misdemeanours): detained defendants 'receive jail sentences that are more than twice as long on average'. Dobbie et al. (Philadelphia and Miami, p. 3): release lowers the chance of being found guilty by 15.6 points; its effect on incarceration is 'small and not precisely estimated' overall (3.0 points) but large for felony and drug cases.

rows.explainer: Detention makes defendants plead guilty to get out, so released defendants are convicted and jailed less. Our judgment: 12 days of sentence avoided per defendant released (0 to 45), about a tenth more of them serving a sentence of some months. Read by every model that counts defendants released before trial; the days come after the case closes.

rows.label: Deaths caused per year of pretrial detention lasting months, as a share of the deaths per year in prison

source.title: charityevals' judgment, anchored on Patterson (2013), The dose-response of time served in prison on mortality: New York State, 1989-2003, American Journal of Public Health 103(3): 523-528

rows.explainer: As jail_mortality_vs_prison, for people held before trial for months (denial of bail, cash bail they can't pay): the deaths in jail still cluster in the first days after admission, before most such detention is decided, but months inside bring most of the cumulative harm to health, work and family that a prison term does. Our judgment: 0.7 of the prison rate per year (0.3 to 1.2). Read by every model that counts months of pretrial detention avoided.

rows.label: Harm to families and children, as a share of the value of a prison-year averted

source.title: Wakefield and Wildeman (2013), Children of the Prison Boom: Mass Incarceration and the Future of American Inequality, Oxford University Press
source.note: Parental incarceration harms children's wellbeing and behaviour and partners' income; no study puts it on the life-satisfaction or death scale of the prison-year itself, so the share is our judgment.

rows.explainer: Partners and children of a person in prison lose income, contact and care: 15% of the value of the prison-year (its life satisfaction and the deaths it causes), from 0 to 40%. Read as a side effect by every model that frees people or keeps them out of prison.

rows.label: Earnings lost after release, as a share of the value of a prison-year averted

source.title: Western (2002), The impact of incarceration on wage mobility and inequality, American Sociological Review 67(4): 526-546
source.note: Prison lowers later wages and wage growth; the life-satisfaction gap of a year inside is measured during the year, so later earnings are outside it. The share is our judgment.

rows.explainer: A year in prison lowers earnings after release (a record, lost work experience), which the life-satisfaction gap measured inside does not cover: 10% of the value of the prison-year, from 0 to 30%. Read as a side effect by every model that frees people or keeps them out of prison.

rows.label: Remaining life expectancy of a person freed around 45 after a long prison term (years)

source.title: Arias and Xu, United States Life Tables, 2022, National Vital Statistics Reports 74(2), Table 2 (males)
source.page: Table 2 (life table for males), age 45-46; the Human Life-Table Database copy of NVSR 74(2)
source.note: US men of 45 have 33.4 years left in 2022 (50: 29.1); people after long prison terms die younger (Patterson 2013), so ours is lower, a judgment.

rows.explainer: People exonerated after long terms are 45 on average when freed: US men of 45 have 33.4 years left (2022 life table), people after 16 years inside fewer: 26 years, from 21 to 31. Turns years of life lost into a share of a death for people freed at these ages (the 40 years of remaining_life_in_prison is for the younger prison population).

rows.label: Years of life lost per extra year in prison, for people already serving long terms

source.title: Patterson (2013), The dose-response of time served in prison on mortality: New York State, 1989-2003, American Journal of Public Health 103(3): 523-528
source.note: Patterson's 2 years per year comes from parolees who served under 2 years on average (terms of up to 10 years) and cannot run on linearly. The gap between the life table at 45 (33.4 years) and the 26 years left to people freed at 45 after 16 years inside (remaining_life_freed_after_long_prison) is about 7.4 years, or 0.46 a year served. Our judgment.

rows.explainer: Each further year inside, for someone already serving a long term, costs less life than Patterson's 2 years for short terms: 0.5 years, from 0.2 to 1.2, matching the life-table gap of people freed at 45 after 16 years (about 0.46 a year). Read by models that free people late in long sentences; the 2-year figure stays for the shorter terms reforms and decarceration avert.
